posts.title: Mixing asagi by hand
posts.excerpt: Our house colour starts as two drops of blue and a spoon of transparent white.
posts.content:
Every colour on the press is mixed on a glass slab with a palette knife. Asagi is our house colour: process blue, a touch of green and a lot of transparent white.

We weigh the first batch and write the recipe on the tin, so a reprint next year matches the first run.

posts.title: Setting a name in lead
posts.excerpt: Thirty minutes at the type case for one line of type.
posts.content:
A name on a card is set letter by letter into a composing stick, upside down and backwards. Spacing is done with thin brass and copper slips.

Workshop guests are always surprised how long one line takes, and how quickly they learn to read backwards.

posts.title: The 1952 platen press
posts.excerpt: The press that came with the shop, still running most afternoons.
posts.content:
Our platen press was built in 1952 and has printed in this room ever since. The flywheel is turned by a small motor now, but the feeding is still by hand.

It prints about eight hundred sheets an hour when everything goes well; most days it is closer to five hundred.

posts.title: Why cotton paper
posts.excerpt: Soft board takes a deep impression without cracking.
posts.content:
Letterpress used to be printed with a kiss: no dent at all. Today people want to feel the letters, and that needs a thick, soft paper.

Our cotton board is 600 g and made from recycled textile offcuts. It takes the impression like clay.
